data.reason: Second review, round two, run because the sixth Codex round died on a usage limit without a verdict. Advisory only: this ticket touches billing and agent actions, so the gate requires a reviewer from the assistant that did not write the work, and only codex satisfies that. Recorded as a return because the findings are real, not to stand in for the review the gate demands. Criterion 2 is judged MET and the foreign-table thread the dying Codex round was pulling is settled against it being a third F29: create policy and enable row level security are both refused 42809 on a foreign table, so including one would make the criterion unsatisfiable rather than unmet, and the exclusion is enforced rather than promised because part 6's revoke covers defaclobjtype 'r' which includes foreign tables. F32 is high and verified here before recording: part 6 revoked the default privileges on tables only, so anon and authenticated still hold EXECUTE by default on every function a later migration creates in public. A security definer function, which is the ordinary Supabase RPC pattern, is born carrying anon=X; anon is refused public.tenants with 42501 and reads both tenants' names through a three-line function; and the repository's own lockdown statement, revoke all on function from public, which part 8 writes five times, leaves anon=X standing and anon still reads. That is F19's defect one object class over, in the file written to close F19, and config.toml names the exposed class as tables, views, sequences and functions where part 6 answered one quarter of it. F33 is the same for sequences, where anon called nextval and setval. F34 is that SEEN-062's acceptance criteria do not carry the digest obligation F31 left with it. F35 to F38 are lower.

findings.claim: Part 6 revokes the default privileges `on tables` only, so anon and authenticated still hold EXECUTE by default on every function a later migration creates in public, and no guard in the suite reads a function privilege at all.
findings.failure_scenario: SEEN-035's approval inbox or SEEN-024's ops console adds `create function public.pending_approvals() returns setof ... language sql security definer`, which is the ordinary Supabase RPC pattern. Measured on the live stack in a rolled-back transaction: pg_default_acl for schema public, defaclobjtype 'f', still reads `anon:EXECUTE authenticated:EXECUTE` from both the postgres and the supabase_admin grantor, so the function is born with proacl `{=X/postgres,postgres=X,anon=X,authenticated=X,service_role=X}`; supabase/config.toml exposes `public` to PostgREST, so it is a POST /rpc/<name> endpoint reachable with the anon key; and no table in public carries relforcerowsecurity (0 of 29, measured), so the function runs as its owner and bypasses every tenancy policy. Executed: anon is refused `select from public.tenants` with 42501 and reads both tenants' names through `public.probe_tenant_directory()`, a three-line security definer function nobody granted anything on. The repository's own lockdown pattern does not close it either: `revoke all on function public.probe_x() from public`, the statement part 8 writes five times, leaves `anon=X/postgres` standing and anon still executes the function; only `revoke ... from anon, authenticated` refuses it 42501. Nothing fails: schema.test.ts filters every default-privilege query on `d.defaclobjtype = 'r'` (line 568), part 6's self-check does the same (lines 275 and 303), and the string `has_function_privilege` appears nowhere in packages/core/db. This is F19's defect one object class over, in the file written to close F19.

findings.claim: The same revoke leaves the default privileges on sequences standing, so anon holds USAGE, SELECT and UPDATE on every sequence a later migration creates in public, and no guard reads a sequence privilege either.
findings.failure_scenario: SEEN-014's ingest or SEEN-021's findings adds a `bigint generated by default as identity` or `bigserial` column, which creates public.<table>_<col>_seq. Measured in a rolled-back transaction: the sequence is born `{postgres=rwU/postgres,anon=rwU/postgres,authenticated=rwU/postgres,service_role=rwU/postgres}`, and as anon I called nextval (accepted, returned 1), read last_value, which is a row count aggregated over every tenant, and called `setval(seq, 1)` (accepted), which makes the next ingest insert collide on the primary key until the sequence catches up, tenant-wide, from a caller who never signed in. pg_default_acl shows defaclobjtype 'S' granting anon SELECT, UPDATE and USAGE from both grantors; part 6 revoked only `on tables`; `relkind = 'S'` appears in no guard in packages/core/db; and supabase/config.toml's own comment names the auto-exposed class as "tables, views, sequences and functions", which is the sentence part 6 answered one quarter of.

findings.claim: The not-buyer-PII classification of the two Message-ID columns is a promise made to SEEN-062, and SEEN-062's acceptance criteria do not contain it, so nothing the next author reads before writing the code carries the obligation.
findings.failure_scenario: SEEN-062 is at status todo and its four acceptance criteria are the definition of done; I read them, and none mentions a Message-ID, a digest or PII, and the word digest does not appear in the file at all. Its author writes the obvious thing and stores the raw Message-ID from the Postmark inbound payload into messages.external_message_id, once per inbound message. That value carries the buyer's sending host to the right of the at sign and a local part their client chose. It is then persisted indefinitely, in cleartext, with no 30-day expiry, because SEEN-083 reads the classification and the classification says Not buyer PII. Nothing detects it: part 7's own comment says so in as many words, "prevention with no detection", and the guard at schema.test.ts:1312 asserts only that the comment states an obligation and names the ticket, never that anybody kept it. That is CLAUDE.md's buyer PII rule broken by construction with the schema's approval. The ticket's Outcome calls this a gap somebody should close; the fix is inside reach, because SEEN-062 is still todo and an amendment to its criteria is the one place the promise would be read.

findings.claim: A foreign table is the one row-bearing relation kind in public whose presence no statement in the migration set and no test forbids, while tables.ts:576 says its rule "is the same as for a materialised view", which part 6 refuses outright.
findings.failure_scenario: A later migration creates a foreign table in public over a reporting warehouse. Part 6's do block raises on a materialised view and on a view without security_invoker and passes silently over relkind 'f'; its privilege strip ran once, when that migration applied, and does not re-run. What then holds is the test guard alone, which I confirmed does catch a later `grant select` to authenticated and a later `grant select (col)` to anon on a foreign table. So the exposure is closed and the rule is not: the migration permits a relation in public whose rows no policy of this database governs, service_role reads it unfiltered, and information_schema.tables reports it as a table of the public schema, measured as 29 BASE TABLE and 1 FOREIGN, while criterion 2's guard has never asked it anything. The asymmetry is worth closing because the next reader is told in tables.ts that the three kinds share one rule, and they do not.

findings.claim: The behavioural cross-tenant probe and the uniqueness fixture still build their table list from relkind = 'r', so the two relation families F29 established disagree between schema.test.ts and the two files beside it.
findings.failure_scenario: A later migration adds a partitioned table carrying tenant_id, RLS enabled and a policy whose clause is added to TENANCY_CLAUSES because it narrows further. schema.test.ts passes it on the catalogue. rls.test.ts's beforeAll (line 1099) and requiredColumns (line 907) list only 'r', so no row of either tenant is ever seeded into the parent and no read is ever made through it, and uniqueness.test.ts's existence check (line 219) would not see it either. The guard F29's round called the answer to a textual check, that a policy which leaks fails because it leaks, is exactly the guard that never runs on the relation kind F29 was about.

findings.claim: The doc comment on MIGRATION_SET_HEADER says "The set is the seven SEEN-008 migrations" where the directory holds eight and every migration header states eight.
findings.failure_scenario: The third review returned this ticket because parts 1 to 3 counted the set at three and so sent the next author away before part 4's per-table privilege boundary. The test written for that reads the count from disk, so it passes, and the prose beside the test now carries the stale number instead. An author reading tables.ts to learn what the set is is told seven, stops at part 7's classification, and never reads part 8's erasure registry, its advisory lock or its self-check, which is the same route the count was made a test for.

findings.claim: The revoke block claims no function here is callable except through its trigger and this migration, and omits seen.refuse_erasure_registry_mutation, the one function the file creates after it; seen.touch_updated_at from part 1 is likewise left at the PUBLIC default.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured: both have proacl null, which is the built-in EXECUTE to PUBLIC, and anon holds USAGE on schema seen from part 1 line 25, so anon can name and call both. They are harmless only because they return trigger and answer 0A000, "trigger functions can only be called as triggers". The next author adds a seen helper that returns something other than trigger, copies the pattern of the functions around it including the omission, and it is callable by anon; no guard in the suite reads a function privilege in either schema, so nothing fails. The statement in the migration is a claim about its own privileges that is false as written, which is the class of defect this ticket named at F22 and F24 and drew a lesson from.
